speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Bill also imposes obligations concerning the reporting of GHG emissions of business facilities, in place of the obligations currently in the Energy Conservation Act.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I have spoken in this House about how climate change poses existential challenges for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are already experiencing its impacts – changing weather patterns, more intense rainfall and rising sea levels.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Singapore is thus an active advocate and contributor to global climate action, as this is the only way to preserve a habitable planet for our children.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is also why we are rallying Singaporeans in this Year of Climate Action.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our Climate Action video has been viewed more than a quarter million times.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are encouraged by the passion and activism of our fellow Singaporeans and businesses doing their part for climate action.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our 2016 Climate Action Plan outlines the climate adaptation measures we are taking to build Singapore’s resilience to climate change, as well as the climate mitigation measures to reduce GHG emissions in every sector through driving energy efficiency, robust transport policies around what we call "car-lite" policies for a "car-lite Singapore" and waste management policies aiming for a "Zero Waste Nation".

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The carbon tax is thus an integral part of this suite of mitigation measures to nudge our industries towards a low carbon footprint.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Put together, it will enable Singapore to meet our commitments under the Paris Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: But climate change also presents new opportunities for our companies.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Under the Climate Action 100+ Initiative, 256 investors managing US$28 trillion in assets have committed to work with companies to reduce emissions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Companies that adopt greener technologies and climate-friendly practices will find it easier to operate and thrive.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: China has already made a strategic choice and stated its ambition to transform its economic development and shift towards a low-carbon economy.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To maintain our competitive edge, Singapore companies must also transform.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Consumers all over the world will soon demand products and services that use the smallest carbon footprint.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, we still have some way to go, as leading jurisdictions, such as Belgium and the Netherlands, achieve annual improvement rates of 1% to 2%.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The carbon tax will incentivise companies to improve energy and carbon efficiency, while giving them the flexibility to take action where it makes business sense.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: My Ministry held a consultation session recently with industry and non-government organisation (NGO) participants.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Many participants agreed on the need for climate action and supported pricing carbon.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is consistent with the views expressed by business leaders worldwide.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of ExxonMobil, Darren Woods, blogged that, "A uniform price of carbon applied consistently across the economy is a sensible approach to emissions reduction.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This would promote greater energy efficiency and the use of today’s lower carbon options, avoid further burdening the economy, and also provide incentives for markets to develop additional low-carbon energy solutions for the future".

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Since the Finance Minister announced the carbon tax at Budget 2017, we have been consulting stakeholders closely on implementation.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To manage compliance costs for companies, the Bill builds on the existing requirements in the Energy Conservation Act (ECA).

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Similar to ECA, the Carbon Pricing Act will be administered by the National Environment Agency (NEA).

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Keeping in mind companies' compliance costs and our international competitiveness, we studied the laws in other carbon pricing jurisdictions, such as the European Union (EU), California and South Korea, to ensure that our requirements are appropriately calibrated and aligned to international practices.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We also took reference from the requirements and associated penalties in relevant domestic legislation, including the ECA, as well as the Income Tax Act and the Goods and Services Tax Act.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have also transferred all the GHG emissions reporting requirements from the ECA to the CP Bill.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Through many rounds of consultations with potentially affected companies, NGOs and the general public since early 2017, we have received constructive and useful feedback to refine the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Part 3 – coverage and definition of facility.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Part 3 of the Bill identifies the persons and business facilities that must be registered under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Facilities from the manufacturing, power generation, water supply and waste management sectors will be covered.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have made refinements to how the ECA defines a "business facility" to provide greater clarity to companies and to align our definition with international practices.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A business facility is a single site where a business activity that involves the emission of GHG and forms a single undertaking or enterprise is carried out.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The "person", which can be a company or other legal person, having operational control over the facility must be registered under the Bill, and will be responsible for fulfilling the obligations under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A "business activity" can be an activity or a series of activities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Bill allows for business activities that are carried out at two or more parcels of land separated from one another to be treated as carried out at a single site in certain instances, including if the activities are under the operational control of the same person and are carried out in an integrated manner and clear dependencies between the activities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Other jurisdictions have similar practices, where separate installations with technical connections or in physical contact, can form a single facility.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We hope that this exception will encourage companies to consider the synergies across plants in order to reap greater emissions reduction and improve resource efficiency.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It will also lower compliance cost as only one emissions report needs to be submitted for a single business facility spanning multiple premises.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Bill imposes obligations in relation to two types of facilities – taxable facilities and reportable facilities.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This threshold does not include the GHG emissions listed in Part 2 of the Second Schedule which I will elaborate on later.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These facilities will have to undertake more rigorous measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) processes and will have a carbon tax imposed on their GHG emissions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We took reference from key jurisdictions, such as the EU and South Korea, in deciding on the threshold level of 25,000 tonnes.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We aim to strike a balance between maximising our emissions coverage while managing the compliance cost for smaller emitters.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A robust MRV regime forms the foundation of an effective CP scheme.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For reportable facilities, the measurement and reporting requirements will be similar to their existing ECA reporting practices, whereas taxable facilities will adhere to a more stringent set of MRV requirements.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Emissions reports for taxable facilities must be submitted annually based on a monitoring plan.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The monitoring plan sets out data management practices to ensure that GHG emissions data is measured and reported accurately and robustly.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The registered person having operational control of a taxable facility will also be required to engage a qualified independent third party, accredited by NEA, to verify the emissions reports.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This provides an independent review of the measurements and reporting of a facility's GHG emissions, akin to a company engaging an external auditor to audit its financial statements.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The details of the carbon tax can be found in Part 5 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The initial rate of S$5 per tonne has been specified in the Third Schedule and can only be amended by an Act of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our carbon tax will be applied uniformly without exemptions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It will take the form of a fixed-price credits-based mechanism.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This means registered persons will pay the carbon tax by surrendering carbon credits equivalent to their carbon tax liability.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These carbon credits can only be bought from NEA at a fixed price.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have designed our carbon tax this way to give us the flexibility to introduce international credits or link to other emissions trading systems, if and when there are opportunities to do so.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, in the initial phase, international credits or offsets will not be allowed as we want our companies to focus on reducing their emissions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: That said, we recognise that companies welcome the potential use of international credits.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We are monitoring the global discussions on the use of and accounting of international credits and will continue to study this issue.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First and Second Schedule – coverage of GHG emissions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The carbon tax will be levied on the direct emissions of six types of GHGs, namely, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs) and sulphur hexafluoride.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These are the six gases that Singapore is required to report under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: To reduce compliance costs, there will be a list of GHG emissions that are excluded from the carbon tax, similar to the practice in other CP jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The list comprises small sources of emissions which have a disproportionately high cost to measure and report compared to the amount of carbon tax collected.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These sources of emissions are typically from ancillary processes and are insignificant compared to a facility's total GHG emissions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The list of excluded emissions is specified in Part 2 of the Second Schedule.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It includes GHGs emitted from fire extinguishers, and HFC and PFC emissions from air-conditioning equipment used for non-manufacturing purposes, such as in office buildings.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Furthermore, we will exclude emissions arising from the use of petrol, diesel and compressed natural gas (CNG).

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Although the excluded emissions are not taxed, registered persons will still be required to measure and report most of this data, using simpler methods to estimate such emissions.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This data will enable us to track whether these emissions have grown over time and review the list of excluded emissions, if necessary.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Bill also provides an avenue for a registered person to appeal to the Minister against NEA's decision pertaining to the deregistration of taxable facilities, approval of verified emissions reports or monitoring plans, or tax assessments and refunds.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These disputes may involve highly technical and specialised industrial processes.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is a significant step to bring us closer to a liveable and sustainable Singapore, where thriving businesses have low carbon footprints and where climate action is a way of life for all.

speaker: The Minister for the Environment and Water Resources (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Through this transformation, our companies will be able to remain internationally competitive and capture opportunities in the low-carbon economy of the future.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill will be a good step forward to get our people to be in sync with the international trend.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We need to position Singapore for a low-carbon future as that will be the new norm.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Taking climate action need not be a tradeoff against economic development.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Rather, we should recognise that taking climate action today is important and can reduce business risk and open new opportunities and growth for businesses, especially in the eco-industry.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It can also spur businesses to move up and upgrade themselves and be more efficient in the use of energy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is a necessary step that will enable Singapore to stay competitive as we move towards a carbon-constrained world.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: During Budget 2018, the Finance Minister announced that support for companies will be enhanced through schemes like the Productivity Grant and EE Fund.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How effective have they been in encouraging improvements in EE?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What outreach efforts are employed to get more companies on board?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, are there any "standard packages" or success stories that the Ministry can recommend to companies that do not know how to go about doing it?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: While charging a flat rate of $5 carbon tax helps simplify matters, companies are concerned about the lack of a clear benchmark.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They are concerned that if the tax fails to reduce carbon emissions, the tax rate will eventually be increased across the board, thus penalising those who have been reducing their carbon emissions and reducing competitiveness overall.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, can we be more open with regard to how the MRV requirements are done?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On this subject, I understand that the reports have been a mandatory requirement even before this Bill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: NEA has been working with companies to familiarise them with the new measurement and reporting requirements on large emitters in the Energy Conservation (Amendments) Act passed last year.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The CP Bill introduces a new requirement for additional third-party verification on emissions reports, which will ensure greater fairness and accuracy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The carbon tax will put a price signal to encourage consumers to reduce their emissions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, improving our EE continues to be a key strategy in reducing our carbon footprint whilst improving our competitiveness.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is, hence, important for companies to be more ambitious in their EE improvements.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The carbon tax and ECA will work hand in hand, together with other mitigation measures, to reduce our emissions intensity and meet our Paris pledge.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With the new Singapore Energy Centre to be launched in early 2019 to explore innovative ideas and develop talent to meet future energy needs, I am confident that this will further elevate our regional and global standing as a leader for eco-solutions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is good news for businesses which will find our nation's reputation stands them in good stead.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government share further details about the Singapore Energy Centre, as well as other future investments in eco-solutions?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: While I am optimistic for businesses, I have some concerns for households.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This may not seem significant but, with the increase in price of water and other items, it will all add up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One major public concern is how it will affect our cost of living.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How to ensure that businesses do not profiteer?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: From the second half of this year, consumers will be free to switch from Singapore Power to other energy providers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is in line with the move to increase competitiveness in the energy solution industry and give consumers the freedom to choose a company whose package complements their principles and budget.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many households and small businesses have been using Singapore Power for a long time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, making the move might be challenging, especially among the elderly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can do more to increase public awareness.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Personally, I have made the Climate Action Pledge, and I am also looking into how to put in place measures to reduce the energy usage of our Community Club in the coming CC upgrading.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope to get more residents on board this worthy initiative.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Reducing reliance on energy is not just for protecting the environment, it also helps to reduce the impact of energy prices on our economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Experiences from other countries have shown that carbon tax can effectively promote companies to save energy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are there any success stories that the Government can share with the companies?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, how would the oil refining industry be affected by the carbon tax, and will the Singaporeans working in this industry be affected as well?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government rebate cover the increase in utility prices?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the event that the carbon tax increases in the future, will the Government increase the rebate amount?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those most endangered are young Singaporeans and future generations of Singaporeans yet unborn.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Paris Accord which Singapore supports represents what is best in the international community, namely, a determination to halt this dangerous slide towards anthropogenic climate change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, as a nation, we need to set a good example to the world community.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a civilised country, Singapore should reject the unfortunate notion, fashionable in some quarters now, that carbon emissions do not cause climate change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The evidence that carbon emissions are causally related to climate change is overwhelming and represents far and away the consensus among scientists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not only is the evidence of carbon emissions accelerating climate change overwhelming, history has shown that nations of the world can find the resolve to act in concert so as to reverse the negative effects of human activity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The best example of this was the damage to the ozone layer caused by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) which was effectively halted by the global agreement on CFCs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Montreal Protocol in 1987, which took effect in 1989, banned CFCs, halons and other ozone-depleting chemicals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ozone levels began to stabilise in the mid-1990s and recover in the 2000s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nations can find the political will to act in unison against the threat to the shared future of humanity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is vital to keep in mind the prospect of success in facing important global challenges like climate change and not to give in to the kind of pessimism that guarantees defeat.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Anthropogenic climate change could bring about great harm to many millions of human beings through practical consequences like rising sea levels, swamping coastal and inhabited areas, increasing frequency of freakish weather events and the spread of infectious diseases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore, being a low-lying island nation, would be particularly vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the rest of my speech, I will make a few suggestions in relation to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Measuring our resilience to climate change recognises the possibility that the world may, indeed, get climate change wrong.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And Singapore needs to plan for that eventuality by ensuring resilience.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, the world was reminded of this possibility when President Trump pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement on Carbon Emissions though one hopes that the US will eventually re-enter the agreement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a scorecard for broader climate change contributions and resilience could be populated with data and published at regular intervals for public debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is worthwhile to do, given the importance of this issue to Singapore and the world, particularly the future generations of Singaporeans who will be the ones who really pay the price if the world gets climate change wrong.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Emissions intensity is one relevant and important indicator.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other indicators of climate change contributions and resilience may include, firstly, our drainage capacity and technologies to withstand possibly higher levels of rainfall in future to avoid flooding and minimise ponding.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The urban heat island effect refers to how certain types of building materials, technologies and urban plans can inadvertently lead to significantly higher temperatures in particular areas of the city.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, the extent to which we maintain our terrestrial fresh water and marine biodiversity so that our nature reserves and marine parks can become sights for sustainable eco-tourism and research.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fourthly, the extent to which we improve and strengthen our local farming sector to better guard against the threat of unpredictable overseas weather patterns affecting our imported food supply.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And, lastly, the extent to which we adopt or even use research and development (R&D) to develop solutions in the fight against vector-borne diseases like dengue that may be worsened by climate change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other than the price, our CP plan would seem to have a number of parallels with the Australian CP plan that was enforced from 2011 to 2014.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, Australia had set its carbon price at A$23 at their plan's inception.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, of course, necessary to balance the goal of disincentivising carbon emissions with the goal of ensuring that our economy has time and resources to adapt to the tax while remaining competitive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, it is prudent to set the price at a low level initially.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having said that, it is not clear if setting the carbon price at such a low level and the pass-through change in terms of end-user prices that that brings about will nudge end-users to substantially change their behaviour with regard to energy conservation or the deployment of carbon-lite energy-efficient technologies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not argue that we should set the carbon price higher at this stage to balance the effect on the economy and the people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, so as to nudge the economic ecosystem towards a smaller carbon footprint in the longer term, which is the goal of any CP regime, I have the following suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Government − and this is my second broad point − consider setting a goal for the share of renewable contribution to total energy production in the longer term?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have called for this in the House previously.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such a goal, even if expressed as arranged, has the effect of focusing minds both in the Government and in the private sector, and may nudge decisions to trial tests and, ultimately, adopt cleaner technologies knowing the tougher measures are inevitable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Note that this is not the same as arguing for subsidising renewable technologies using devices like feed-in tariffs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is useful to announce a longer-term renewables target because that sends a signal that the regime for incentivising renewables and disincentivising carbon-intensive technologies will gradually and, over time, become more rigorous even if the timeframe is fairly long.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may embolden and encourage companies thinking of investing in new and innovative renewal projects, would-be entrepreneurs thinking of setting up startups in the field, and workers considering developing their skills and careers in the renewables field.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Presumably, the goal here is to nudge the economy into lower world-class levels of carbon use per unit of gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This could, in the longer term, bring about new greener possibilities for the economy and help nudge economic actors towards adopting them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One criterion for funding projects could be that they testbed new technologies in Singapore, so that the knowhow from deploying and maintaining such technologies resides in Singapore and diffuses through our workers and companies, creating knowledge that will enhance our economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The economic benefits so derived, such as new investments and jobs, may even increase tax revenues and turn out to be revenue-positive in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such broad economic measures could be coupled with administrative measures to nudge economic actors towards new technology adoption.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, developers could be required to install a certain minimum capacity for solar panels on roofs, with exceptions given on a case-by-case basis, for those buildings with minimal rooftop sunlight or which have the case for setting aside some rooftop space for other uses like rooftop gardens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The notion of publishing carbon emissions data is not novel.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many large global companies publish emissions data and this is a trend that is likely to grow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Publishing the data from large emitters may be in line with where global trends are heading anyway.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, it is possible that some of the global companies registering emissions data under the CP Bill would be publishing global submissions data in any case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, this goes beyond the datasets released by the National Climate Change Secretariat (NCCS) for broad sectors like transport industry, power generation and buildings at the moment.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is clear when I hear the Second Reading speech of the Minister that the Ministry has clearly thought of and studied the possibility of an optimal mix of solutions in technology and policy for what is currently the best position that we could take, as well as going forward, what we need to take if we need to achieve that 2030 commitment.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But allow me, Mr Speaker, to ask a couple of questions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that these new regulatory measures, including the MRV for taxable or reportable facilities, may incur costs, and that may have an impact on industry competitiveness.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Companies may not regard EE improvements as a priority.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, they may regard these new requirements as an additional compliance cost when they are trying to maintain product quality.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In ensuring product specifications are met, more energy could be needed to complete the manufacturing process, as an example.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Some experts have suggested that there could be a misalignment between the Government's policies and business sentiments.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: With these new policy changes, Mr Speaker, much of the responsibility will be on these companies to step up and adhere to the enhanced regulations under both ECA as well as the CP Bill, if it becomes law.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If done satisfactorily and in line with international standards, Singapore will be in a good position to participate in the external carbon markets in the future.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is important, Mr Speaker, given that international market mechanisms that are currently being developed under the Paris Agreement commitments and rulebook are expected to play a significant role in facilitating countries in meeting their climate commitments and goals.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Council for the EU recently released a diplomatic statement calling for urgent action.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They say that the window for global warming to reach the 2-degree Celsius target, the upper temperature limit that was agreed and committed to in Paris, is "fast closing", and they ask parties to the Paris Agreement to create "a uniform regime with rules applicable to all".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, however, Mr Speaker, developing countries, including China, are calling for a bifurcated, two-tier rulebook, with less stringent reporting requirements for developing countries.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This will be one of the key issues for negotiators to thrash out at the 24th Conference of the Parties (COP24) to the United Nations (UN) Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) later this year in December.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this as well because we are not just an early adopter of this uniform approach at that time, but through the commitment that we see in this Bill before us, we are an early adopter of the commitments as a whole in the Paris Agreement, and I celebrate this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The CP Bill is welcomed as a useful tool to help us meet our obligations under the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With regard to the Bill, I would like to raise several points.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This will allow us to know whether the carbon tax is effective in abating consumption, and whether there is a need to either finetune the tax amount or postpone a further increase.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Third, I hope the Government can bear in mind the potential cost increase in business.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: By that, I mean, beyond the carbon price itself, including the indirect costs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Have we worked hard to ensure that the compliance and administrative costs are not too onerous?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will companies have to hire dedicated and specific resources to see through this, in addition to their core operation?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps the Government or NCCS can also help beef up our companies' capabilities by providing some technical support or assistance in the short run, so that companies can develop their own capabilities to do compliance in a very cost-effective way.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Fourth, I hope that the Government can also communicate the carbon price design and necessary procedures early on, so that companies can invest early to be compliant.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Given the fact that most of our petrochemicals industry's output are exported, and their competitors based in other countries may not need to price in their carbon emission, is there anything more we can do to mitigate their challenges overseas?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding the concerns I have, I agree with the approach of embarking on carbon tax, rather than other alternatives, such as carbon trading.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Carbon trading is ideal in countries where there are low-cost as well as high-cost ways of reducing emissions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Low-cost ways could include environmentally friendly forestry and farming practices.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, carbon trading encourages the society to do two things: one, to reduce carbon emission and, two, find a way for companies to negotiate among one another and to find the cheapest way to achieve the reduction.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, I would like to point out that for Singapore, our carbon emission companies are concentrated in, I believe, petrochemical, power-generation and manufacturing sectors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, they are quite homogenous in their carbon emission approaches.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We do not have forestry and farming industries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, there is very little arbitrage opportunities for us from different industries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, there is always the option of buying carbon credits from outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But I have real concerns about the integrity and effectiveness of some of these carbon credit schemes and we have to watch very carefully how this evolves in real life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In comparison, I like the clear CP approach; it is clear and effective, and it can be easily rolled out, and the revenues can be directly applied to better our society.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Though Singaporeans understand the need to embrace a low-carbon economy by reducing GHG emission, Singaporeans are still concerned that companies will pass down the cost of the carbon tax to the consumers, therefore, increasing the cost of goods and consumer spending.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of the carbon tax will incur cost that affects industry competitiveness.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As a small nation that relies heavily on trade and foreign investment, how is the Government going to ensure that the economy remains competitive with the introduction of the carbon tax?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we help SMEs to be energy-efficient and to go green with the use of renewable energy?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we stop exploitation of consumers by some unscrupulous companies?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While it is important to reduce carbon emission for climate change, the companies generally do not regard EE as a priority and may regard the new requirements as an extra step to maintain product quality.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of viewing the carbon tax as an additional cost, how do we encourage companies to bear in mind the EEs they get to reap at the process or product design stage, if they pay attention to low- or no-carbon emission processes?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With the verified emission reports submitted by companies, would the Government analyse the data and look into areas where companies with high carbon emission can do better and provide the required advice or suggestions so that companies can act on proactively?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Government can also consider engaging the company more regularly to follow up on their high emission, or even include conducting an audit on their carbon dioxide emission level.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will some of this highly classified information from the companies be kept safe under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA)?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is it simple enough for companies, especially SMEs, to understand?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are there industries or processes that are exempted from this carbon tax?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I think earlier the Minister did say that some of the areas are exempted.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, it is good for the Government to provide predictable carbon tax rate increases over time.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This allows companies to better manage their operating cost, and workers, especially those in the petrochemical industries, will be minimally affected by this additional cost if such cost can be factored in earlier, in a predictable manner.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Government should also provide incentives for companies to adopt renewable energy sources and for those that innovate their processes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The carbon tax revenue generated can be used to further the cause of "Going Green" by investing in appropriate relevant "green" projects using the revenue generated.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For consumers, we should discourage the use of plastic bags in a robust manner.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: After all, reducing carbon emission is the responsibility of every one and it starts with "I".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Climate change is one of the most serious problems of our time, and the consequences of unchecked climate change for every country, including Singapore, are likely to be grave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In Singapore, industries are the largest emitters of GHG.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is thus an important and necessary step to manage Singapore’s carbon emissions and is aligned with our commitment to the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, many green groups have raised queries and concerns with me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Please allow me to share some of them and seek a few short clarifications on details of the implementation of our carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If this is so, companies would thus have to make an accurate estimate of how much emissions the facility would produce for the reporting period and buy the corresponding number of credits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The main concern here is whether any unused credits can be used in the next reporting period.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If unused credits do expire before the next reporting period, I am concerned that facilities that have over-bought credits may be compelled to use less energy-efficient technologies, so as to use up the credits they have already purchased and are unable to transfer or sell.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is also possible that companies in this situation would feel no incentive to reduce emissions as they have bought more than enough credits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Whichever the case, it would go against the primary objective of this Bill, which is to promote more energy-efficient methods of production to drive down carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, greener alternatives for industries and power generation will require substantial investments and all-round support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The green community is heartened to know that the funds from the tax will go back into the green initiatives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With a new stream of funds available, there are hopes that greater support can be given to promote the use of clean energy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I must confess that prior to being on the council, my awareness of environmental issues was low.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I still have much to learn but, at least now, I am more conscious about the effect my actions have on the environment and the need to take steps to reduce my carbon footprint.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The consciousness to protect our environment is not just a lofty ideal but an essential value, which should be present in all of us.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This value should be nurtured, and we need to continue to educate people, young and old, about the role each of us plays in protecting the environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The introduction of this Bill is an opportunity to further inform and edify people about the environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This Bill is premised on the desire and need to create a sustainable future for our children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addressing the common feedback and concerns about the Bill, we should continue to remind the public and various stakeholders of this pertinent vision.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At the same time, there also needs to be support to the people, businesses and stakeholders in adjusting to the changes put in place and the knock-on effects of the same.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The carbon credit system has also been lauded for allowing for some flexibility.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There were some queries as to whether there is a plan to move towards a carbon trading system in the future where companies with low emissions could sell off their credits to larger emitters.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It does allow for flexibility, but we do need to think about the overall impact to the effort in reducing emissions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also note that the Minister had made reference to the International Credit System and that Singapore will carefully study the feasibility of linking our carbon tax framework to other CP jurisdictions with high environmental integrity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The implementation of this Act, if it comes to pass, will clearly change the way businesses are run.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There will be administrative work to be done, mechanisms which need to be put in place to track emissions, as well as auditing to be carried out to ensure compliance.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Given that this is a completely new regime that the businesses are facing, would the Government be providing support, perhaps in the form of business consultancy, to help the affected entities manage the change?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Following from this, perhaps the expected revenue from the carbon tax could be channelled towards supporting or incentivising companies to stay through the course in their efforts to reduce emissions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: While we show the stick, it is also useful to dangle the carrot to encourage positive development in this sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is a lot of potential to harness green innovation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But some further funding may need to be allocated to this cause.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I would like to know from the Minister if there will be any new or enhanced grants in place to encourage green innovation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Aside from the concerns and feedback from the businesses, we have also heard a lot of comments from the public about their fear on how the carbon tax will impact the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There has already been a buzz about increases in prices of food and drinks at coffee shops.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is necessary to note that in our effort to protect the environment, that we do not inadvertently hurt the very people whom we are protecting the environment for.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   We often talk about the importance of protecting the environment; preserving it for future generations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, this is not about just paying lip-service but rather something that we should embody.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is an essential value which should be present in all of us and we must take actions in our daily lives to execute this vision.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Bill before us today is an important measure that can encourage people to be more concerned about the impact of our lives on the environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our daily activities usually generate carbon that will pollute the air and destroy the environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Most of the carbon in the air is emitted by certain industries.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Under this new legislation, certain companies will be taxed based on their carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The money that needs to be set aside for this carbon tax will nudge these companies into paying more attention to carbon emissions and find new ways to be more productive and environmentally-friendly.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many have voiced concern that the cost of living will rise due to this carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We really need to take the opportunity to continue educating the public so that everyone can embrace changes positively and work towards developing more eco-friendly habits.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Speaker, Sir, this year being designated our Year of Climate Action, it is fitting that we, as a nation, take meaningful and significant steps towards reducing our carbon footprint and GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For too long, GHG emissions had been an externality on our environment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is timely that our Government has chosen to implement various policies, including CP, to "internalise" the externalities of GHG emissions, so that the costs and benefits will impact those who choose to incur them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I certainly support CP to incentivise both industries and consumers to do the right things to reduce our contribution to GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The transition period should be bearable as the taxes will result in slightly higher prices for consumers but not enough to impact our economy's competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Imposing carbon tax on major GHG emitters is a wise move by the Government.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree that this measure can help reduce environment pollution and hence help do our part for the environment and the next generation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All electricity consumers, big or small, will somewhat be affected by the rise of electricity tariff.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the increase is estimated to be bearable for the general households.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe all of us will work together to reduce electricity usage, which is good for the environment and can save money as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.58 pm until 3.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Last week, The Business Times published an article entitled "A powerful, effective strategy to combat climate change" which featured the views of top executives of companies and professional associations on the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I was heartened by their strong support for the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many executives recognised that pursuing environmental sustainability and economic growth are not a matter of tradeoffs, but a strategy to stay competitive; they can do good and do well at the same time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Paul Henaghan, Vice President from Dell DMC, noted, and I quote, "Industries need to look beyond the perceived economic loss from taxation and recognise that it ultimately contributes to the long-term prosperity of companies".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Damien Dhellemmes, Country President of Schneider Electric Singapore, said and I quote, "Going green can, in fact, lead to greater economic growth in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We strongly believe that sustainability is the end game of any company in today's world".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is why we are introducing the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As our companies are nudged towards more carbon-efficient and greener practices, they will strengthen their competitive edge and thrive in a low-carbon global future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To Asst Prof Madhev Mohan's query, the carbon tax should not be viewed in isolation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It works in tandem with the comprehensive mitigation measures that we have developed to reduce emissions and meet our obligations under the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This package has been carefully designed, taking into consideration our international competitiveness as well as our pledge, and will be reviewed regularly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our initial carbon tax level of S$5 per tonne cannot be directly compared with that of other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: While they may have higher headline carbon prices, they often give significant exemptions to particular sectors and companies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These effectively pay a lower carbon price than the published rate.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Rather than imposing differing tax levels on different sectors and companies, we have opted for a simple and transparent carbon tax with no exemptions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This maintains a fair and consistent price signal to incentivise emissions reduction across the entire economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I also want to assure the House that we are mindful of our international competitiveness when introducing this tax, given that we are an export-oriented economy, as highlighted by Mr Henry Kwek and Ms K Thanaletchimi.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Together with MTI, the Economic Development Board (EDB) and NCCS, my Ministry and NEA have consulted companies extensively over the past year on the design of our carbon tax framework.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our review will take into account international climate change developments, our progress towards our climate pledge and our economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As highlighted by Mr Henry Kwek and Ms Rahayu Mahzam, we are mindful of the need to manage compliance costs, which was also a key feedback from companies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These requirements take reference from international standards like the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and GHG Protocols, which are used by many companies for corporate sustainability reporting.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This approach streamlines requirements and aligns with international practices.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Second, we have identified a list of excluded emissions so that companies need not incur disproportionately high costs to measure and report these small emissions sources.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Third, NEA is actively growing the pool of third-party verifiers in Singapore to ensure that companies can access competitive offerings.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA has been organising briefings to familiarise companies with the new MRV requirements and carbon tax obligations and will continue to help companies build up their capability.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The detailed MRV requirements will be made publicly available.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam also asked if there is a plan to move towards an emissions trading scheme (ETS) in the future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For a small domestic market like Singapore, a carbon tax could achieve the same objective as an ETS in a simpler way.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Nonetheless, we recognise that there may be benefits in linking our market with other jurisdictions in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is a complex endeavour, as Ms Rahayu Mahzam has pointed out, and we are still studying the feasibility.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will need to build up key capabilities both in the Government and companies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We, therefore, decided to introduce the Fixed-Price Credit-Based (FPCB) system as this will put in place the key building blocks should we decide to link our market to other jurisdictions in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue to monitor international developments and consult companies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the FPCB mechanism.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There is no expiry date on the credits in this initial phase.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Nevertheless, companies have told us that they are likely to buy the required credits only after they receive the notice of tax assessment, so as not to tie up their liquidity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, the scenario whereby companies operate their plants in a less efficient manner in order to, as Mr Louis Ng has stated, "use up unused credits", is highly unlikely.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Leon Perera also asked if the Government will share the data from the emissions reports, and Ms Thanaletchimi asked about the measures we have to ensure data security.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As the emissions reports contain commercially-sensitive information, they will not be shared publicly.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have strict provisions in the Bill to ensure the confidentiality and security of the data reported.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That said, I note that the Members are concerned about tracking the effectiveness of our policies in lowering our energy consumption and efficiency, and emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We also regularly report our emissions to the UNFCCC and will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: On average, the additional U-Save rebates will cover the expected increase in electricity and gas expenses arising from the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will help HDB households to adjust to the carbon tax, as they reduce their utilities consumption over time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will assess the impact of the carbon tax at a later stage and review the need to extend these rebates.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: More importantly, we want to encourage energy-saving habits among households on a sustained basis.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are working with the community on a Lamp Replacement Programme to assist 1- and 2-room HDB households to replace their lamps with more energy-efficient Light Emitting Diode (LED) ones.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: NEA will also be organising an Energy Savings Challenge this year to raise awareness on energy conservation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I would also like to assure Ms Thanaletchimi and Ms Rahayu Mahzam that Government agencies will work closely with the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) and the Competition Commission of Singapore (CCS) to monitor the market for unfair pricing and coordinated price hikes which are anti-competitive.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: CASE will look into feedback of any alleged profiteering.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As Members have highlighted, a key reason for the carbon tax is to encourage our companies to transform and ready themselves for the low-carbon economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To achieve this, I agree with Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that we must be more ambitious and bolder in improving EE.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Many developed countries are achieving an EE improvement rate of 1% to 2% per year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The industrial sector, which accounts for about 60% of Singapore’s GHG emissions, has been a key focus of our efforts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Last year, we amended the ECA to enhance the frameworks and tools to support companies’ EE improvement.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: One new requirement is for new industrial facilities and major expansion projects to undergo reviews at the design phase to identify and incorporate EE opportunities at the start of the project, thereby avoiding more expensive retrofitting and operational disruption later on.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This year, we are moving the CP Bill to provide the added motivation – the motor fuel if you like – to spur companies to actively pursue emissions reduction.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Government has been providing support to continue to improve EE and many have forged ahead.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Globalfoundries, a semiconductor company, has been innovating and investing in new technologies to improve EE and reduce emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, it redesigned the combustion chamber in its thermal abatement units and reduced its liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) consumption by 31%.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This resulted in annual cost savings of about S$260,000 and an annual carbon abatement of about 640 tonnes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Another role model is Chevron Oronite Pte Ltd which has consistently achieved EE improvement rates above the industry average.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To improve EE, it installed a boiler system to recover waste heat from its thermal-oxidiser for steam generation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It also installed a mechanical vapour recompression system to lower the energy use of its new manufacturing unit.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These projects have resulted in energy savings of S$1.8 million and carbon abatement of 4,800 tonnes each year.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Members have asked what the Government is doing to support companies in this transition to a low-carbon future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Existing EE incentive schemes, such as PG (EE) and E2F will be enhanced.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Enhanced support will also be extended to SMEs to encourage them to improve their EE, including basic measures, such as upgrading to more efficient lighting.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: More support will go to projects that achieve greater emissions abatement, beyond basic enhancements.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Leon Perera has asked whether part of the revenue from the carbon tax will be used to provide loans to companies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: EDB has been piloting an EE Financing Programme whereby companies that are not able to afford the upfront costs of EE projects can apply for loans through a third-party financier.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The potential benefits of such a programme are that industrial facilities will not have to pay for the upfront costs of these projects but can still enjoy part of the energy savings.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Part of the risk is transferred to the third-party financier.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Beyond financial support, the Government will also grow the wider industrial EE ecosystem in Singapore to develop greater expertise in the energy services sector.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Initiatives include engaging Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to train and upskill energy services professionals, and working with professional bodies, such as the Institution of Engineers Singapore to develop Chartered Engineer certification for EE professionals.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At the same time, NEA officers have been and will continue to engage the companies to help them to identify areas for EE improvements.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Besides driving EE improvement, the carbon tax will help spur investment in and take-up of low-carbon solutions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked if the Government can provide incentives for companies to adopt renewable energy sources.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Government’s policy is to ensure that energy, regardless of source of generation, is correctly priced to fully reflect the cost of generation and let the market work out the equilibrium.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Instead of providing subsidies, what we have done is to invest in the R&D of renewable, clean energy technologies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We set up the Solar Energy Research Institute of Singapore (SERIS) in 2008 to conduct R&D on solar technologies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: One of its projects is a collaboration with the Renewable Energy Corporation (REC) Group to develop high-performance solar cells, which I understand, is among the world’s highest-performing solar cells.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are also studying the deployment of solar panels beyond our rooftops onto our water bodies.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In 2016, the Public Utilities Board (PUB) launched the largest testbed at Tengeh Reservoir.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Addressing intermittency issues and ensuring grid stability are important as we increase solar deployment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Energy Market Authority (EMA) and Singapore Power launched the Energy Storage System testbed in 2016 to better understand the feasibility of deploying grid-level energy storage technologies locally.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I assure Mr Louis Ng that the Government will continue to support and invest in such R&D efforts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the impact on the refining sector in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In my interactions with our refinery companies, I have been impressed by their bold and transformational moves.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Since 2000, ExxonMobil has spent about US$8 billion to develop low-carbon technologies and are a global leader in carbon capture and storage technology.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These oil giants are showing us the way by taking destiny in their own hands and transforming earlier, rather than later, to stay competitive and maintain their lead in the low-carbon global economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Leon Perera asked whether we regularly measure our climate change resilience.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To ensure that Singapore is well-prepared for climate change, we have set up an interagency Resilience Working Group (RWG) that is responsible for studying and monitoring Singapore’s vulnerabilities to the effects of climate change, such as sea level rise, and developing appropriate response measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our climate scientists are also plugged into relevant global scientific forums that develop climate change projections.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Our adaptation measures are reviewed whenever there are new findings.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Lastly, Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan also asked about our position in the development of the Paris Rulebook, given the positions taken by the EU and China.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As one would expect in a multilateral framework, negotiations are complex.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Publicised positions may be transitional and do not reflect the landing points.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Singapore participates actively in these negotiations to get countries to focus on a fair and consistent implementation of their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), what they commit to reduce and mitigate GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: At the end of the day, for the Paris Agreement to work, all countries must meet their commitments that they have committed to.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will continue to participate actively to this end.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, Singapore’s active involvement in previous rounds had been impactful.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We must continue to be active and impactful because climate change is an existential issue for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The carbon tax has been deliberated carefully and extensively within the Government.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We have also made a concerted effort to consult and engage the industry.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Bill is an important step forward, not only in encouraging industry to do their part for the climate, but also in readying our economy and strengthening our competitiveness as the world transitions to a low-carbon economy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, I call on Members of the House to give their support to this Bill.
